segments.text: In season 1, we covered user stories how
to write them using the as a I want to
so that format. But a user story without
acceptance criteria is incomplete.
Acceptance criteria is what tells the
development team exactly when a user
story is done. In this video, I will
show you exactly what acceptance
criteria is, why it matters, and how to
write it using the most powerful format
in agile given when then. Let's get into
it.
Acceptance criteria are the specific
conditions that must be met for a user
story to be considered complete and
accepted by the business. Think of them
as the definition of done for each
individual requirement. Without
acceptance criteria, developers don't
know exactly what to build. Testers
don't know exactly what to test and
stakeholders don't know exactly when to
sign off. Acceptance criteria removes
all ambiguity from a requirement and
replaces it with clear testable
conditions. Here is why acceptance
criteria are non-negotiable in any agile
project. First, they prevent
misunderstandings.
Without clear criteria, developers and
stakeholders often have completely
different ideas of what done means.
Second, they drive testing. Every
acceptance criterion becomes a test
case. Well-ritten criteria make the
tester's job straightforward. Third,
they control scope. They define the
boundaries of the user story. What is in
and what is out. Fourth, they enable
sign off. Stakeholders can only formally
accept a story when it meets the agreed
criteria. And fifth, they reduce rework.
Issues caught through criteria before
development are 10 times cheaper to fix
than those found after. The most
powerful and widely used format for
writing acceptance criteria is given
when then, also known as the Girkin
format. Here is how it works. Given
describes the initial context or
precondition. What is true before the
action happens? When describes the
action or event that triggers the
scenario. What does the user or system
do? Then describes the expected outcome.
What should happen as a result? For
example, given the user is on the login
page. When they enter a valid username
and password and click login, then they
are redirected to their account
dashboard within 2 seconds. This format
is clear, structured, and directly
testable.
One user story can and usually should
have multiple acceptance criteria
scenarios covering the happy path, the
alternate paths, and the error paths.
The happy path is the main success
scenario. Everything works as expected.
The alternate path covers valid but
different flows. For example, logging in
with a remembered device. And the error
path covers what happens when something
goes wrong. For example, entering an
incorrect password. As a rule, always
cover at least three scenarios for every
user story, happy path and alternate
flow, and at least one error condition.
This ensures your requirements are truly
complete. Let me bring this to life with
a real world example. User story. As a
registered user, I want to reset my
password so that I can regain access to
my account. Now, let us write the
acceptance criteria. Scenario one, happy
path. Given the user is on the forgot
password page. When they enter a valid
registered email and click submit, then
a password reset link is sent to that
email within 2 minutes. Scenario two,
invalid email. Given the user is on the
forgot password page. When they enter an
email not registered in the system, then
an error message is displayed saying
email address not found. Scenario three,
expired link. Given the user has clicked
an expired reset link, when they try to
reset their password, then they are
shown a message saying the link has
expired with an option to request a new
one. A common confusion in agile teams
is the difference between acceptance
criteria and definition of done. Here is
the simple explanation. Acceptance
criteria are specific to each individual
user story. They describe the conditions
that make that particular story
complete. The definition of done is a
team level checklist that applies to
every story. It includes things like
code reviewed, unit tests written,
deployed to test environment, and
documentation updated. Think of it this
way. Acceptance criteria says this
specific story is done when these
conditions are met. The definition of
done says every story must also pass
these general quality checks before it
can be released. Here are five tips to
write outstanding acceptance criteria.
One, write criteria before development
starts. Never leave acceptance criteria
to be written after the story is built.
Two, make every criterion testable. If
you cannot write a test case for it, it
is too vague. Three, avoid technical
language. Acceptance criteria should be
readable by both business stakeholders
and developers. Four, keep each
criterion focused on one outcome, one
scenario, one outcome. Never combine
multiple results in a single criterion.
And five, involve stakeholders in
writing them. The best acceptance
criteria are written collaboratively
with the product owner and key business
users, not by the BA alone. Here are the
best tools for writing and managing
acceptance criteria. Jira is the most
common. Write your given when then
scenarios directly in the acceptance
criteria field of each user story
ticket. Confluence is excellent for
storing shared acceptance criteria
templates and guidelines the whole team
follows. Azure DevOps has built-in
acceptance criteria fields in the work
item form. Widely used in Microsoft
stack organizations. Cucumber is a
dedicated tool for behavdriven
development. It runs your given when
scenarios as automated tests and notion
or Google Docs work well for smaller
teams who need a simple accessible place
to document criteria.
To summarize, acceptance criteria define
exactly when a user story is done. Use
the given when then format. It is clear,
structured, and directly testable.
Always cover the happy path, alternate
paths, and error paths. Write criteria
before development starts and involve
your stakeholders in the process.
Mastering acceptance criteria is what
separates a good BA from a great one. It
is the difference between a story that
gets accepted first time and one that
bounces back from the development team
three times. If you found this video
helpful, please subscribe to Business
Analysis Simplified for more advanced BA
content every week. See you in the next
